summary.text: The Columbian exchange was the widespread transfer of plants, animals and diseases between the Americas and Afro-Eurasia from the late 15th century on.
It is named after Christopher Columbus and is related to the European colonization and global trade that followed his 1492 voyage.
Old World diseases caused an 80 to 95 percent reduction in the Indigenous population of the Americas, while American crops such as potatoes and maize became important around the world.

facts.label: Term coined
facts.value: First used in 1972 by historian Alfred W. Crosby

facts.label: Disease toll
facts.value: 80 to 95 percent fall in the Americas' Indigenous population

facts.label: American crops
facts.value: Maize, potatoes, tomatoes, tobacco, cassava, chili peppers

facts.label: Old World crops
facts.value: Rice, wheat, sugar cane and livestock

facts.label: Potato
facts.value: Before 1500, not grown outside South America

items.prompt: A root crop from South America reached Africa in the 16th century. What role did it come to play there?

options.label: It stayed a garden curiosity eaten only by wealthy families
It gradually replaced sorghum and millet as the most important food crop
It was grown for export only, never eaten locally
It was replaced by sorghum and millet within a few years

items.explain: Cassava was introduced from South America by the Portuguese and gradually replaced sorghum and millet as Africa's most important food crop.

items.prompt: Why did European cities and populations change after a crop from the Andes became a staple food?

options.label: Potatoes contributed to population growth and to rising urbanization
Potatoes were mainly exported to Asia, leaving Europe short of food
Potatoes caused a famine across Europe in the 1700s
Potatoes had little effect on the number of people in Europe

items.explain: Potatoes became an important staple, contributing to an estimated 12 to 25 percent of population growth in Afro-Eurasia and to much of the increase in urbanization between 1700 and 1900.

items.prompt: Why did the Indigenous population of the Americas fall so sharply after contact?

options.label: Their crops failed because of imported insects alone
They moved in great numbers back across the Atlantic
Communicable diseases of Old World origin spread among them
They were replaced only by wars between rival kingdoms

items.explain: Communicable diseases of Old World origin resulted in an 80 to 95 percent reduction in the Indigenous population and near extinction in the Caribbean.

items.prompt: A farmer plants imported seeds on purpose, while a town elsewhere is struck by an illness no one brought on purpose. What does this show about the exchange?

options.label: Every transfer was planned by the Crown from the start
Every transfer happened by accident with no human choice
Only diseases moved, while plants and animals stayed put
Some exchanges were deliberate, while others were unintended

items.explain: Some of the exchanges were deliberate while others were unintended.

items.prompt: Crops carried to new regions often gave somewhat higher yields for a limited time. Why?

options.label: The soil there held more minerals than farmers could ever use
The crops traveled widely, but their native fungi at first did not
Farmers there had more tools than farmers at home
The new regions had warmer weather for a few decades

items.explain: Because crops traveled widely but at least initially their endemic fungi did not, yields were somewhat higher for a limited time, a "yield honeymoon".

items.prompt: In the first three centuries after Columbus, which group crossed to the New World in greater numbers?

options.label: Europeans, far more than Africans
Both groups, in about equal numbers
Africans, far more than Europeans
Neither, since most travel went the other way

items.explain: The number of Africans taken to the New World was far greater than the number of Europeans moving there in the first three centuries after Columbus.

paragraphs.heading: What it was
paragraphs.text: The Columbian exchange was the large-scale movement of plants, animals and diseases between two halves of the world, starting in the late 1400s. On one side was the New World, the Americas; on the other was the Old World, meaning Africa, Europe and Asia. It takes its name from Christopher Columbus and is tied to the colonies and trade that grew up after his voyage of 1492. Some of these transfers were made on purpose, and others happened by accident.

paragraphs.heading: Where the name comes from
paragraphs.text: The American historian Alfred W. Crosby, of the University of Texas at Austin, coined the phrase in his 1972 book The Columbian Exchange. Other historians and journalists quickly took it up. Crosby set out to map the biological and cultural transfers between the two worlds. He carried that work further in a 1986 book, Ecological Imperialism.

paragraphs.heading: Before 1492
paragraphs.text: Scientists agree that people first reached the Americas from Siberia thousands of years ago, bringing domestic dogs with them. After that there is little evidence of contact between the two worlds. Norse visits to Greenland, Newfoundland and Vinland around the 10th and 11th centuries left no known mark on the Americas. Many scientists think Polynesians may have met South Americans around 1200 and taken home the sweet potato. Only with Columbus's first voyage in 1492 did the exchange really begin.

paragraphs.heading: Crops that fed the world
paragraphs.text: Potatoes, maize, cassava, sweet potatoes, tomatoes, chili peppers and tobacco went out from the Americas to become major crops worldwide. Before 1500, nobody grew potatoes outside South America. By the 1700s they were common in Europe and important in India and North America, and by one estimate they lie behind 12 to 25% of Afro-Eurasia's population growth from 1700 to 1900. The Portuguese brought cassava to Africa in the 16th century, where it slowly overtook sorghum and millet as the main food crop. They also carried chili peppers and potatoes to India, where both became central to the cooking.

paragraphs.heading: Crops going the other way
paragraphs.text: Rice, wheat, sugar cane and farm animals from the Old World became important in the Americas. Coffee, arriving around 1720 from Africa and the Middle East, and sugarcane, brought from the Indian subcontinent to the Spanish West Indies, became the main export crops of large Latin American plantations. European planters growing rice depended on the skills of enslaved Africans. Those Africans brought their know-how in controlling water, milling and winnowing to the fields.

paragraphs.heading: Disease and forced migration
paragraphs.text: The exchange also carried sickness. Diseases from the Old World cut the Indigenous population of the Americas by 80 to 95 percent, and in the Caribbean they nearly wiped it out. People crossed as well, some free and some enslaved, heading from the Old World into the New. Over the first three centuries after Columbus, far more Africans were taken to the Americas than Europeans went there.

paragraphs.heading: A short-lived bonus
paragraphs.text: Crops travelled far, but at first the fungi that attacked them at home stayed behind. For a time, yields in the new lands were somewhat higher, an effect called ecological release or a yield honeymoon. Pathogens have kept spreading as the world has grown more connected, though, and yields have slipped back toward their endemic levels.
